body_es:
El patrón publicación/suscripción (pub/sub) desacopla a los emisores de mensajes (publishers) de sus receptores (subscribers) a través de un intermediario llamado broker o canal. A diferencia de las colas punto a punto, en pub/sub cada mensaje publicado en un topic puede ser entregado a múltiples suscriptores simultáneamente.

Los conceptos clave son: topic o canal (nombre lógico al que se publican los mensajes), publisher (componente que emite mensajes sin saber quién los recibe), subscriber (componente que se registra para recibir mensajes de un topic) y broker (intermediario que gestiona las suscripciones y las entregas).

Las ventajas son el desacoplamiento total entre productores y consumidores, la facilidad de escalar el número de consumidores de forma independiente y la capacidad de añadir nuevos subscribers sin modificar el publisher.

Los sistemas pub/sub más usados son Apache Kafka, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Redis Pub/Sub y MQTT para dispositivos IoT. En Python, el patrón puede implementarse con clases simples que mantienen un diccionario de handlers, como se muestra en el ejemplo.
body_en:
The publish-subscribe (pub/sub) pattern decouples message emitters (publishers) from receivers (subscribers) through an intermediary called a broker or channel. Unlike point-to-point queues where one consumer processes each message, pub/sub delivers each published message to every subscriber registered to that topic.

Core concepts: a topic is a named channel; a publisher emits a message to a topic without knowing who will receive it; a subscriber registers interest in a topic and is called when messages arrive; the broker maintains the subscription registry and handles delivery.

Pub/sub enables zero-copy fan-out: one publish event triggers N independent processing pipelines. It also allows adding new consumers at runtime without any modification to the publisher, which is its principal advantage over direct service calls.

Popular systems include Apache Kafka, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Redis Pub/Sub, and MQTT for IoT. In Python, the pattern is naturally expressed as a class holding a dict of topic → list[handler]. Fan-out is a for-loop over that list, which is exactly what production brokers do internally.

Subscribed analytics_handler to topic "user.signup"
Subscribed audit_handler to topic "user.signup"
Subscribed alert_handler to topic "payment.failed"
Subscribed audit_handler to topic "payment.failed"
Publishing to "user.signup": {'event': 'user.signup', 'user': 'bob'}  (2 subscriber(s))
  [Analytics] logged event: user.signup
  [Audit]     stored record: {'event': 'user.signup', 'user': 'bob'}
Publishing to "payment.failed": {'event': 'payment.failed', 'order': 55}  (2 subscriber(s))
  [Alert]     paging on-call for payment.failed
  [Audit]     stored record: {'event': 'payment.failed', 'order': 55}
source: Enterprise Integration Patterns — Hohpe & Woolf, Publish-Subscribe Channel — https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/PublishSubscribeChannel.html
